listen_text: Section. Introduction. If Sigma is a modal system, then the soundness theorem establishes that if Sigma derives formula A , then formula A is valid in any class class C of models in which all instances of all formulas in Sigma are valid. In particular that means that if logic K derives formula A then formula A is true in all models; if logic K T derives formula A then formula A is true in all reflexive models; if logic K D derives formula A then formula A is true in all serial models, etc. Completeness is the converse of soundness: that K is complete means that if a formula A is valid, formula A is derivable , for instance. Proving completeness is a lot harder to do than proving soundness. It is useful, first, to consider the contrapositive: K is complete if and only if whenever formula A is not derivable , there is a countermodel, that is, a model model M such that formula A is not true throughout model M . Equivalently (negating formula A ), we could prove that whenever not formula A is not derivable , there is a model of formula A . In the construction of such a model, we can use information contained in formula A . When we find models for specific formulas we often do the same: for example, if we want to find a countermodel to p implies necessarily q , we know that it has to contain a world where p is true and necessarily q is false. And a world where necessarily q is false means there has to be a world accessible from it where q is false. And that's all we need to know: which worlds make the propositional variables true, and which worlds are accessible from which worlds. In the case of proving completeness, however, we don't have a specific formula A for which we are constructing a model. We want to establish that a model exists for every formula A such that not formula A is not derivable in system Sigma . This is a minimal requirement, since if not formula A is derivable in system Sigma , by soundness, there is no model for formula A (in which Sigma is true). Now note that not formula A is not derivable in system Sigma if and only if formula A is Sigma -consistent. (Recall that Sigma does not derive not formula A in system Sigma and formula A does not derive falsity in system Sigma are equivalent.) So our task is to construct a model for every Sigma -consistent formula. The trick we'll use is to find a Sigma -consistent set of formulas that contains formula A , but also other formulas which tell us what the world that makes formula A true has to look like. Such sets are complete Sigma -consistent sets. It's not enough to construct a model with a single world to make formula A true, it will have to contain multiple worlds and an accessibility relation. The complete Sigma -consistent set containing formula A will also contain other formulas of the form necessarily formula B and possibly formula C . In all accessible worlds, formula B has to be true; in at least one, formula C has to be true. In order to accomplish this, we'll simply take all possible complete Sigma -consistent sets as the basis for the set of worlds. A tricky part will be to figure out when a complete Sigma -consistent set should count as being accessible from another in our model. We'll show that in the model so defined, formula A is true at a world—which is also a complete Sigma -consistent set—if and only if formula A is an element of that set. If formula A is Sigma -consistent, it will be an element of at least one complete Sigma -consistent set (a fact we'll prove), and so there will be a world where formula A is true. So we will have a single model where every Sigma -consistent formula A is true at some world. This single model is the canonical model for Sigma . End section.

listen_text: Section. Lindenbaum's Lemma. Lindenbaum's Lemma establishes that every Sigma -consistent set of formulas is contained in at least one complete Sigma -consistent set. Our construction of the canonical model will show that for each complete Sigma -consistent set Delta , there is a world in the canonical model where all and only the formulas in Delta are true. So Lindenbaum's Lemma guarantees that every Sigma -consistent set is true at some world in the canonical model. Theorem. Lindenbaum's Lemma. If Gamma is Sigma -consistent then there is a complete Sigma -consistent set Delta extending Gamma . End theorem. Proof. Let formula A sub zero , formula A sub one , and so on be an exhaustive listing of all formulas of the language (repetitions are allowed). For instance, start by listing object p sub zero , and at each stage n is greater than or equal to one list the finitely many formulas of length n using only variables among object p sub zero , and so on, object p sub n . We define sets of formulas Delta sub n by induction on n , and we then set Delta equals the union over n of Delta sub n . We first put Delta sub zero equals Gamma . Supposing that Delta sub n has been defined, we define Delta sub n plus one by: Displayed expression. Delta sub n plus one equals Delta sub n union the singleton containing formula A sub n, if that union is Sigma consistent; otherwise it equals Delta sub n union the singleton containing not A sub n. End cases. End displayed expression. Now let Delta equals the union of Delta sub n for n from zero to infinity . We have to show that this definition actually yields a set Delta with the required properties, that is, Gamma is a subset of Delta and Delta is complete Sigma -consistent. It's obvious that Gamma is a subset of Delta , since Delta sub zero is a subset of Delta by construction, and Delta sub zero equals Gamma . In fact, Delta sub n is a subset of Delta for all n , since Delta is the union of all Delta sub n . (Since in each step of the construction, we add a formula to the set already constructed, Delta sub n is a subset of Delta sub n plus one , so since the subset relation is transitive, Delta sub n is a subset of Delta sub m whenever n is less than or equal to m .) At each stage of the construction, we either add formula A sub n or not formula A sub n , and every formula appears (at least once) in the list of all formula A sub n . So, for every formula A either formula A belongs to Delta or not formula A belongs to Delta , so Delta is complete by definition. Finally, we have to show, that Delta is Sigma -consistent. To do this, we show that (a) if Delta were Sigma -inconsistent, then some Delta sub n would be Sigma -inconsistent, and (b) all Delta sub n are Sigma -consistent. So suppose Delta were Sigma -inconsistent. Then Delta derives falsity in system Sigma , that is, there are formula A sub one , and so on, formula A sub k belongs to Delta such that Sigma derives the nested conditional from A sub one, through A sub k, to falsity . Since Delta equals the union of Delta sub n for n from zero to infinity , each formula A sub i belongs to Delta sub n sub i for some n sub i . Let n be the largest of these. Since n sub i is less than or equal to n , Delta sub n sub i is a subset of Delta sub n . So, all formula A sub i are in some Delta sub n . This would mean Delta sub n derives falsity in system Sigma , that is, Delta sub n is Sigma -inconsistent. To show that each Delta sub n is Sigma -consistent, we use a simple induction on n . Delta sub zero equals Gamma , and we assumed Gamma was Sigma -consistent. So the claim holds for n equals zero . Now suppose it holds for n , that is, Delta sub n is Sigma -consistent. Delta sub n plus one is either Delta sub n union the set containing formula A sub n if that is Sigma -consistent, otherwise it is Delta sub n union the set containing not formula A sub n . In the first case, Delta sub n plus one is clearly Sigma -consistent. However, by the proposition on consistency facts the consistency alternative for a formula and its negation , either Delta sub n union the set containing formula A sub n or Delta sub n union the set containing not formula A sub n is consistent, so Delta sub n plus one is consistent in the other case as well. End proof. Corollary. Gamma derives formula A in system Sigma if and only if formula A belongs to Delta for each complete Sigma -consistent set Delta extending Gamma (including when Gamma equals the empty set , in which case we get another characterization of the modal system Sigma .) End corollary. Proof. Suppose Gamma derives formula A in system Sigma , and let Delta be any complete Sigma -consistent set extending Gamma . If formula A does not belong to Delta then by maximality not formula A belongs to Delta and so Delta derives formula A in system Sigma (by monotonicity) and Delta derives not formula A in system Sigma (by reflexivity), and so Delta is inconsistent. Conversely if Gamma does not derive formula A in system Sigma , then Gamma union the set containing not formula A is Sigma -consistent, and by Lindenbaum's Lemma there is a complete consistent set Delta extending Gamma union the set containing not formula A . By consistency, formula A does not belong to Delta . End proof. End section.

listen_text: Section. Determination and Completeness for K. We are now prepared to use the canonical model to establish completeness. Completeness follows from the fact that the formulas true in the canonical model for Sigma are exactly the Sigma -derivable ones. Models with this property are said to determine Sigma . Definition. A model model M determines a normal modal logic Sigma precisely when formula A is true throughout model M if and only if Sigma derives formula A , for all formulas A . End definition. Theorem. Determination. formula A is true throughout canonical model M superscript Sigma if and only if Sigma derives formula A . End theorem. Proof. If formula A is true throughout canonical model M superscript Sigma , then for every complete Sigma -consistent Delta , we have formula A is true at Delta in canonical model M superscript Sigma . Hence, by the Truth Lemma, formula A belongs to Delta for every complete Sigma -consistent Delta , whence by the complete-consistent-set characterization of provability (with Gamma equals the empty set ), Sigma derives formula A . Conversely, if Sigma derives formula A then by the proposition listing properties of complete Sigma consistent sets the deductive closure clause for complete Sigma consistent sets , every complete Sigma -consistent Delta contains formula A , and hence by the Truth Lemma, formula A is true at Delta in canonical model M superscript Sigma for every Delta belongs to world set W superscript Sigma , that is, formula A is true throughout canonical model M superscript Sigma . End proof. Since the canonical model for K determines K, we immediately have completeness of K as a corollary: Corollary. The basic modal logic K is complete with respect to the class of all models, that is, if formula A is valid then logic K derives formula A . End corollary. Proof. Contrapositively, if logic K does not derive formula A then by Determination formula A is not true throughout model M superscript logic K and hence formula A is not valid. End proof. For the general case of completeness of a system Sigma with respect to a class of models, for example, of KTBfour with respect to the class of reflexive, symmetric, transitive models, determination alone is not enough. We must also show that the canonical model for the system Sigma is a member of the class, which does not follow obviously from the canonical model construction—nor is it always true! End section.
